p: Monday, March 28, 2061. 5:30 AM. Daylight saving time had come two weeks ago and taken the mornings with it, so Sam drove out to the stand in the dark again, with the heater on high and the gas bill in his shirt pocket, folded around the number he'd written under minus nine on Friday night. 7740-112.
Wendell was in the blockhouse with the thermos lid on his knee. He didn't look around. Sam set the gas bill on the console between them, number side up.
Wendell looked at it for a while. Same family, he said. Older revision. Different poppet spring.

I worked a stand in 2034. So did a lot of people. He picked up the gas bill, folded it back along its crease, and handed it over. The lady who wrote that in green knows more about that number than I do. Ask her. She'll say she can't tell you. Ask her anyway. Then, before Sam could say anything else, You didn't drive out here at five for that. Quinn says you're doing estimates today.

Wendell reached under the console and came up with a shoebox. In it were pocket notebooks, the narrow kind with a spiral at the top, forty or fifty of them, held together in bunches by rubber bands that had gone soft with age. He took off one band and fanned the covers. Each had two dates written on it in black marker and a stand number.
Every test I ever ran, he said. Front of each page, what somebody told me it would take. Back of the page, what it took. He put the band back on. I want them back.

By seven the program room had become what Quinn called the big room, which meant every table pushed together and every wall papered over. On the long wall she'd taped up the work packages from February, four hundred and eighty of them, one card each. On the table she'd set out three pads of sticky notes in three colors, green, yellow, and red, and a sign in her neat capitals: THREE NUMBERS. NOBODY WRITES ONE.

The people who came weren't the leads. Sam had asked the leads to send the people who'd actually do the work, and most of the leads had, so the room was full of people who had never built this ship, because nobody had. Two stack technicians from the Breather lab, one of them twenty three, who kept checking her phone like it might excuse her. The lander integration crew in their high bay coveralls. A woman from the electrochemistry team who brought her own calculator. Rafa sent four software engineers and came himself, which nobody had expected. Hana sent her deputy and came at nine, which everybody had.
The twenty three year old raised her hand before anybody had said anything. What if I don't know how long it takes?
Then your red's big, Quinn said. That's information too.

By 8:15 the cards on the wall had started to grow colored tails. Over the doors the countdown clock said 692. Sam's phone buzzed once with a message from Garrett. On my way down. Bringing finance. Also, the agency's new AI scheduling assistant is going to run Halcyon this week. Hale's office loves it. G.
Ruth's Console Log, page three: a very pretty chart.

Ruth's console log. Petrel Flow. L Minus 327 Days. July 20 2034. oh seven hundred, first integrated schedule review. new scheduling software. every bar a different color. administrator says it looks like a quilt. oh eight fifteen, critical path runs through prop qual. isol VLV cycle tests, 3 campaigns, 14 weeks. oh eight thirty, program wants 4 weeks back. options: second shift on the stand, or overlap VLV campaign 3 with stage integration. oh nine oh five, chose both. oh nine ten, prop objects. wendell on the loop: if campaign 3 finds something, it's already bolted in. oh nine twelve, overruled. noted his objection. he asked me to note it twice. noted it twice. thirteen hundred, new chart printed. 4 weeks of float on the last bar. very pretty. seventeen thirty, L minus 327. wendell's truck still in the lot.

Wendell was forty two. I'd known him three months. I wrote his objection down twice because he asked me to, and I remember thinking that was a strange thing for a man to want, and I understand it completely now. He wanted it on the record that somebody had said it. I've read the 0912 line more times than I've read my own wedding vows, and I was married for thirty one years.

This page is about the schedule, which the ECO calls R8, plan and manage schedule. The enablers start where page two left off: prepare a schedule based on the selected development approach, coordinate with other projects and operations. Then the ones this page is really about. Estimate project tasks, milestones, dependencies, story points. Utilize benchmarks and historical data. Create the schedule, baseline it, execute the schedule management plan, analyze the variation.

Start with who estimates. The people who'll do the work estimate it, because they know the work, and because a number you wrote yourself is a number you'll fight for. Check them against history: what this kind of work took the last time anyone did it. That's what a test conductor's notebooks are. Front of the page, the guess. Back of the page, what happened. Most of an estimator's skill is knowing which side of the page they're looking at.

You'll meet the estimating methods by name on the exam. Analogous estimating uses a similar past project as the basis, scaled by judgment. It's quick and rough, useful early. Parametric estimating uses a statistical relationship, so many hours per kilo, so many days per test cycle, and it's as good as the relationship. Bottom up estimating builds the estimate from the work packages and rolls it up, and it's slow and the most accurate of the three. Agile teams estimate in story points, a relative measure of size and difficulty, and forecast from how many points they actually finish per iteration. Nobody's method is the truth. Each one is a way of being less wrong.

How the exam asks it. When the question asks who should estimate, pick the people doing the work, with history and expert judgment as checks. A number handed down by management or finance is the trap.

A single number is a lie with good manners. Every estimate is a range, and when you ask somebody for one number, what you get is the most likely value with the uncertainty sanded off. The schedule then treats it as fact, and the uncertainty comes back later as a surprise.

So ask for three. Optimistic, the duration if things go well. Most likely, the one they'd bet on. Pessimistic, the duration if the plausible bad things happen. Then combine them. The simple average, (O M P) 3, is the triangular estimate, and it's the formula the PMBOK Guide shows under multipoint estimating. The Guide also lists PERT, and PERT's formula is the beta estimate, (O 4M P) 6, which leans toward the most likely value. The standard deviation for one activity is (P minus O) 6.

Work one through, because the exam will make you. The Breather's acceptance test: optimistic 3 weeks, most likely 4, pessimistic 11. PERT: (3 16 11) 6 30 6 5.0 weeks. Triangular: (3 4 11) 3 6.0 weeks. Standard deviation: (11 minus 3) 6 1.33 weeks.

Look at what that tells you. Most likely was 4. The expected value is a full week longer, because the bad tail is long. When the pessimistic number sits far from the other two, the work has a cliff in it somewhere, and the person estimating knows where. Ask them. About two thirds of the time a duration lands within one standard deviation of the PERT estimate, here 3.67 to 6.33 weeks, and about 95 percent of the time within two, here 2.33 to 7.67. Those percentages assume a normal curve, and nothing on a stand at two in the morning is normal, so treat them as a way of talking about confidence.

For a whole path, you don't add the standard deviations. You add the variances, which are the standard deviations squared, and take the square root of the sum. Two activities with standard deviations of 3 and 4 weeks give a path standard deviation of 5, the square root of 9 plus 16. A long path is less uncertain than its pieces added up, because the pieces don't all go wrong at once. Usually.

How the exam asks it. Read the formula the question asks for. "Beta" or "PERT" means (O 4M P) 6. "Triangular" or "simple average" means (O M P) 3. Don't add standard deviations along a path; add variances.

An activity network is the work with its dependencies drawn in. Most links are finish to start: B can't start until A finishes. There are three others, start to start, finish to finish, and start to finish, the last one rare enough that you'll mostly meet it on the exam. A lead lets a successor start early. A lag makes it wait, the way concrete has to cure, or a chamber has to pump down.

Then you do two passes. The forward pass goes left to right and finds the earliest each activity can start and finish. Early start is the largest early finish of everything feeding it. Early finish is early start plus duration. The backward pass goes right to left from the end date and finds the latest each activity can start and finish without moving the end. Late finish is the smallest late start of everything it feeds. Late start is late finish minus duration.

Total float is late start minus early start, or late finish minus early finish. It's how long an activity can slip without moving the project's end date. Free float is how long it can slip without delaying the early start of anything that follows it: the earliest early start among its successors, minus its own early finish. Free float can be zero when total float isn't, because the slack belongs to the path, and the activity at the head of the path is sharing it with the ones behind.

The critical path is the longest path through the network, the one that sets the end date. On it, float is zero, if the end date is the one the network calculates. Slip anything on it and the end moves. Paths with a little float are near critical, and you watch them, because a week's slip turns them critical. Here's a practical rule I learned too late: tell every owner where they sit. People who know they have three weeks of float don't panic. People who don't know they're critical don't hurry.

One more thing. The critical path is wherever the arithmetic puts it, and that's often somewhere people weren't looking. On Petrel it ran through propulsion, and everybody knew it. On Halcyon, you'll see.

How the exam asks it. Expect to do a forward and backward pass on a small network. Write ES, EF, LS, LF on each box. The path with zero float is critical. If two paths tie for longest, both are critical.
Sooner or later somebody wants the date earlier. There are two honest ways to shorten a schedule without cutting scope, and the exam wants you to know which costs what.

Crashing adds resources to activities on the critical path to shorten them: another shift, more people, faster shipping. It costs money. To choose, you compute each activity's cost slope, (crash cost minus normal cost) divided by (normal duration minus crash duration), and you buy the cheapest week on the critical path first. Then you recalculate, because the critical path can move once you've bought a week, and you buy the next cheapest week on whatever is critical now.

Worked through: plant assembly normally takes 5 weeks for $2.0 million and can be crashed to 4 weeks for $2.5 million. The slope is $0.5 million divided by 1 week, $500,000 per week. Lander integration, 3 weeks for $1.5 million or 2 weeks for $1.85 million, is $350,000 per week. Control software, 8 weeks or 6, $1.0 million or $1.4 million, is $200,000 per week, the cheapest week on the table, and it's worthless here because the software isn't on the critical path. Shortening something with float shortens nothing. Buy the lander week.

Fast tracking does activities in parallel that were planned in sequence. It costs little money up front and it adds risk, because the later activity starts on the assumption that the earlier one will come out fine. If it doesn't, you redo work, and rework is how fast tracking turns out slower than not fast tracking. Fast track things whose outcome you're fairly sure of. Never fast track the thing whose job is to tell you whether you're wrong.

That's the 0905 line. I chose both. We put the stand on a second shift, which was crashing, and the crew was tired. We overlapped the third valve campaign with stage integration, which was fast tracking a test, and the only thing a test is for is to find out. When the third campaign found something, the stage was integrated, and taking the valve back out cost more weeks than we'd bought. That's not quite what happened. It's close enough that I'm not going to tell you the rest of it on this page.

How the exam asks it. Crash the critical activity with the lowest cost slope first, and never an activity with float. If the scenario says the work carries high rework risk or tests something unproven, fast tracking it is the wrong answer.

A schedule that's right about the work and wrong about the people is wrong. The ECO's R4, plan and manage resources, has two enablers that sound obvious: define and plan resources based on requirements, and manage and optimize resource needs and availability. Availability is the one that kills you.

A resource calendar shows when each person, team, or facility can actually work: holidays, training, shifts, a stand down for its seal change, a test conductor who can be in one state at a time. Build them before you trust any schedule, because a schedule laid out without them assumes everybody works every day and nothing ever breaks.

When resources are overcommitted, you have two tools, and the exam will ask you to tell them apart. Resource smoothing moves activities only within their float, so the end date doesn't change and the critical path doesn't move. Use it first. Resource leveling adjusts start and finish dates to fit the resources you actually have, even when that pushes the end date out and changes the critical path. Use it when smoothing can't fix the conflict, and say plainly what it did to the date.

And watch for the single point of failure. Any person who is the only one who can do a critical thing is a risk to the project and to that person, who will be asked to give up every weekend until they quit. Spread the knowledge before you need it spread. Cross training is cheaper than any schedule recovery I ever bought.

How the exam asks it. If the question says the end date can't move, smoothing. If it says resources are fixed and the date may move, leveling. A resource calendar is the answer to "the schedule assumed people were available when they weren't."

The ECO says PMI studied artificial intelligence as one of the trends it hadn't addressed before, and used it as an input to the job analysis behind the new exam. In the tasks themselves it shows up as data work. R1 asks you to estimate work effort and resource requirements, and to collect and analyze data to make informed project decisions. Informed is the word to circle.

An AI scheduling tool will build you a network in minutes that would take Quinn a week, and it'll find sequences you'd never have tried. Some of them will be good. It will also assume whatever its inputs assume, which is usually that every resource is available every day at full capacity, that every test passes the first time, and that the activities it was never told about don't exist. It doesn't know Wendell has a seal change in his notebook. It can't. Nobody typed it in.

So treat an AI schedule the way you'd treat any other estimate from a source that doesn't do the work. Pull out its assumptions and write them down. Test them against the resource calendars and against the estimates of the people who'll do the work. Keep what survives, and say where the tool helped. The project manager stays accountable for the schedule, whoever or whatever drafted it, and you can't hand the accountability to a tool the way you can hand it a calculation.
I had a scheduling program in 2034 that drew bars in eleven colors. It was the most persuasive thing in the building, and it didn't know anything that we hadn't told it. Neither does yours.

How the exam asks it. If an AI tool produces a schedule or estimate, the best answer validates its assumptions and inputs with the team before using it. Adopting it as is, or banning it outright, are the distractors.
When it slips, and when it breaks.

R9 is evaluate project status: develop metrics, assess current progress, measure and update them, communicate status. For a schedule, the honest report says how far each piece has moved against the baseline, whether that movement is on the critical path, what float is left on the paths that aren't, what the end date forecast is now, and what you're doing about it. A slip inside float is still a slip. It's spent float, and float is a project resource, and the next person who needs it will want to know it's gone.

Percent complete across the board is the report people send when they don't want to say any of that. A program that's 61 percent complete everywhere except one activity on the critical path is late, however good 61 looks.

B4 is remove impediments and manage issues. Recognize when a risk becomes an issue: the thing in the register that was going to happen has happened. Then evaluate its impact, prioritize it, pick an intervention, and work it with the people who can help, the same day if you can. A risk gets a review. An issue gets a phone call. In agile language an impediment is anything blocking the team, and the servant leader's first job each morning is to find out what those are and go get them out of the way.

How the exam asks it. For status questions, the best report states variance against the baseline, its effect on the critical path and end date, and the plan. "All green because the end date holds" hides spent float.

P3, lead the project team. Establish expectations at the team level. Empower the team. Solve problems. Represent the voice of the team. Determine an appropriate leadership style. A critical path chart on a wall changes how people work under it. Some of them will hurry. The good ones will hurry until they hurt themselves.

Servant leadership is the style the exam reaches for most often, and it's less soft than it sounds. You find out what the team needs, you remove what's in their way, and you carry their reality up to the people who set the dates, so they don't have to carry the dates down alone. A team that's afraid makes mistakes, and on a ship mistakes have mass. Pace is a safety decision. Make it with them.

And P2, manage conflicts. Find where the conflict comes from, look at its context, and agree on a resolution. The exam names five ways people handle conflict: collaborating or problem solving, which works the actual problem until both needs are met; compromising, where each side gives something up; smoothing, which plays up agreement and plays down the difference; forcing, where one side wins; and withdrawing, which walks away. Collaborating is usually best when there's time and the stakes are real. Then write down the ground rule you agreed on, so the same fight doesn't happen every Monday.
That's page three. Wendell was right, and I had a very pretty chart. Write down the objections. Write them down twice if anyone asks you to.

How the exam asks it. For a team under schedule pressure, the servant leader listens, removes obstacles, and sets a sustainable pace with the team. For a conflict between leads, collaborating on the underlying need is the usual best answer.
Decision one. Front of the page.

Monday, March 28, 8:40 AM. Garrett came in with a man from finance who carried a laptop open in both hands, like a tray. The man from finance set it on the end of the table and turned it so the room could see. It was the 2058 bid: every work package Tallgrass had priced to win the contract, with a duration beside each one in a column labeled BASIS OF ESTIMATE.
These priced the contract, Garrett said. The ARA accepted them. We don't need four hundred people guessing on sticky notes. We have numbers.

Quinn looked at the column. Then at the wall, where the stack technicians' cards had grown red tails nearly twice as long as the bid numbers. The twenty three year old was looking at her own card very hard.

Wendell's shoebox sat at Sam's elbow with the rubber bands on. Sam had read three notebooks over coffee. On the front of one page, in 2052, somebody had told Wendell a thermal vacuum test would take nine days. On the back it said twenty two.
The stack cards have red tails nearly twice as long as the bid numbers. Where should the durations come from?
A. Have each package owner give a three point estimate and check it against the notebooks.
B. Load the 2058 bid durations and their basis of estimate into the schedule as is.
C. Have Quinn scale every duration from the last stage program by mass and test count.
D. Give each team a stretch target and ask it to commit to beating that number by June.

Sam thanks the man from finance and asks him to stay, because the bid is useful as a check, and it is. Then he opens Wendell's shoebox on the table. Front of the page is the estimate. Back of the page is what happened. I want both. The owners write their three numbers. Quinn pairs each card with the nearest thing in the notebooks or the stand logs, and where the bid and the history disagree by more than half, the owner explains it out loud. The twenty three year old explains hers in a voice nobody can hear, and then again louder. Garrett leaves at eleven. At four he sends one line: Why are your numbers longer than mine? Quinn answers it with a photo of one notebook page, front and back.

That's a go. The people who'll do the work estimate it, because they know it and because they'll own the number. Benchmarks and historical data are how you check them, which is an R8 enabler in so many words. A range carries the uncertainty a single number hides.

Tuesday, March 29. The Breather's acceptance test would be run in a chamber in Albuquerque, at Rio Puerco Electrochemical, which built the stacks. The chamber could pull down to Mars surface pressure and chill to sixty below, and only one person at Rio Puerco had ever run a full stack in it. Her name was Paloma Benavidez. She came on the screen at ten from a lab with a whiteboard behind her that said DO NOT TOUCH PUMP 2 in three languages.
Garrett had stayed for this one. Ms. Benavidez, how long is the acceptance test? One number. I've got investors who can't read a range.
Four weeks, she said, too fast. Then, after a second, If the stacks behave.

Quinn asked her for three numbers. Paloma looked off screen at somebody, then back. Three weeks if everything went right. Four most likely. Eleven if a stack tripped at pressure and they had to warm the chamber, pull it, rebuild it, and pump down again. It's happened. Once. In the qualification unit.
Paloma gave three numbers. What goes in the schedule?
A. Schedule eleven weeks, her pessimistic number, and release any time the test doesn't use.
B. Schedule four weeks, Paloma's most likely number, and log the stack trip as a risk.
C. Schedule six weeks, the simple average of her three numbers, with the spread beside it.
D. Schedule five weeks, the PERT estimate of her three numbers, with its standard deviation.

Quinn does it on the whiteboard while Paloma watches. Three plus four times four plus eleven, divided by six: five weeks. Eleven minus three, divided by six: one and a third. So five. Most of the time, somewhere from three and two thirds up to six and a third. Garrett asks what most of the time means, and Quinn tells him two times in three, and he writes that down, which surprises everybody. Paloma says, Nobody's ever put my eleven in a schedule without yelling at me. Sam asks her what makes a stack trip. She talks for twenty minutes, and Quinn writes the risk register entry while she's still talking.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Three point estimating captures the uncertainty, and the PERT formula weights the most likely value while still counting the tail. Reporting the standard deviation tells people how sure you are. Then ask about the pessimistic number, because that's where the risk lives.

Wednesday, March 30. The ARA's scheduling assistant had been given every file Halcyon had ever sent the agency, and at 7:02 AM it sent back a schedule. Hale's chief of staff forwarded it with a note: The Director has seen this. It's very encouraging.

It was beautiful. Twenty two thousand activities, resequenced, color coded by subsystem, with the departure burn on February 4, 2063, two weeks ahead of the plan, and three weeks of float in front of it. It had found real things, too. It ran two habitat thermal tests in parallel that nobody had thought to pair, and it saved four days of chamber time in Albuquerque by reordering the stack checkouts.
Garrett had it up on the big screen when Sam walked in. February 4. With float. The agency's own machine says it.

Quinn had found the assumptions on page 340 of the appendix. She'd printed that page and nothing else. All resources available 100 percent of scheduled time. Calendar: 7 day weeks. No facility maintenance windows provided. Test outcomes assumed nominal. Under that she'd written, in pencil, Wendell at Watkins and Albuquerque the same week in May. Stand seal change missing. Nobody gets sick.
The agency's machine says February 4, with float. What should Sam do with that schedule?
A. Set the assistant's schedule aside in favor of the team's own bottom up estimates.
B. Send Hale both schedules, the assistant's and Quinn's, and let her choose the baseline.
C. Have Quinn rerun the assistant on the real calendars and estimates before anyone uses it.
D. Rebaseline on the assistant's schedule and lock in the three weeks of float it found.

It takes Quinn and two of the software engineers until Friday. They feed the assistant the real calendars: five day weeks, the seal change, Wendell's one body, Paloma's one body, the stack line's actual shifts, and the most likely test outcomes instead of perfect ones. The new run puts the burn on February 18, inside the window, with no float in front of it. It keeps both of the good ideas. The paired thermal tests survive. So do the four days in Albuquerque. Sam sends Hale one page with both schedules side by side, what the assistant assumed, what's true, and the two things it found that the team adopted, with credit. Hale's chief of staff calls. So the machine was wrong. The machine was fast. It was right about two things nobody here saw. It didn't know anything we didn't tell it.

Exactly right. An AI schedule is an input like any other estimate. Collect and analyze the data behind it: pull out its assumptions, test them against resource calendars and the estimates of the people doing the work, and keep what holds up. You stay accountable for the schedule. Say where the tool helped.

Thursday, March 31. Quinn ran the forward and backward passes by hand first, on butcher paper on the big room floor, on her knees, with the new estimates. She said the software lied faster than she did, so she liked to know what the answer was before it told her.

For two years everybody at Tallgrass had known that the critical path ran through the stand. It was the thing the building said about itself. With the new numbers it didn't. It ran through a vacuum chamber in Albuquerque: stack fabrication, plant assembly, the Breather's acceptance test at Mars pressure, and lander integration, with zero float from end to end.
The stand had four weeks of float.
The software release had three weeks of float. The install kit had four. Crew training, far down the paper, had six.
Sam stood over the paper for a long time. Who do we tell? Quinn said.
The critical path isn't where everyone thought. How should Sam share what they found?
A. Keep the weekly reviews on the stand and add Albuquerque to the monthly report.
B. Post the network with every path's float on it and tell each owner where they sit.
C. Tell every team it's on the critical path to keep the whole program's pace up.
D. Publish the critical path to the leads and keep the float figures between him and Quinn.

The butcher paper goes up on the big room wall, and a clean version goes to every lead by noon. Each owner gets one line: you're critical, or you have three weeks of float, or four, and here's who's behind you. Paloma calls from Albuquerque an hour later. We're the critical path? The whole ship? This month. She's quiet. Then I want to be on the Monday call. Every Monday. The software team, three weeks of float, stops working Saturdays, and Rafa says so out loud in the hall as if he'd been waiting years to.

That's a go. The critical path is wherever the arithmetic puts it, often somewhere nobody was looking. Show it, show the near critical paths, and tell every owner their float. Critical owners hurry for the right reason. Owners with float stop panicking. Float you hide gets spent by accident.

Thursday, March 31, 6:30 PM. Quinn stayed late to put the resource calendars into the network, which nobody had ever done for Halcyon, because, she said, nobody had ever asked the network to know that people go home.

At 7:15 she found it. The week of May 16, Wendell was scheduled in two places. At Rio Puerco in Albuquerque, four hundred and fifty miles south, where Paloma wanted the most experienced test conductor in the program sitting the Breather's first pump down. And at Stand 2 in Watkins, where the departure stage's next qualification firings, the valve included, needed him at the console, because he was the only person who'd been there the day it twitched.
He's one guy, Quinn said. I checked.

The Albuquerque test was critical. The stand campaign wasn't. The baseline had laid it in at its late dates, in May, but its early start was April 18, so it had four weeks it could sit anywhere inside. Garrett's scheduling software had a button labeled LEVEL ALL, and Quinn's cursor was sitting on it.
Wendell is needed at two sites the same week, and Quinn's cursor is on LEVEL ALL. What should Sam do?
A. Pull the stand campaign forward to its April 18 early start, still inside its float.
B. Run the software's resource leveling across the program and take the date it gives.
C. Assign a habitat test conductor to the stand campaign and send Wendell to Albuquerque.
D. Have Wendell cover both sites that week, flying between them on alternate days.

Quinn moves the stand campaign up to its early start, the week of April 18, which is still inside its float window, and the end date stays where it was. Wendell sits the stand in April and the Albuquerque pump down in May. Quinn writes it up in two lines for the leads: what moved, why, and that nothing critical did. Hana reads it and pulls up the April weather history for Watkins, which nobody asked her to do, and frowns at it. April out there, she says, and doesn't finish the sentence. Wendell, told he's being moved, says, Nobody's ever checked I was one person.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Build the resource calendars, then smooth: move noncritical work within its float so the end date and critical path hold. Level only what smoothing can't resolve, and report what it did to the dates. Spending float is a real cost, so say so.

Friday, April 1. Sam flew to Albuquerque on the first flight, because it was the critical path, and because he wanted to see it. Rio Puerco Electrochemical was a long tan building near the river with cottonwoods behind it just starting to leaf. The chamber was a steel cylinder you could stand up in, with a round door like a bank vault's and a sign on it that said PUMP 2: ASK PALOMA.

Paloma was thirty four and talked fast. She showed him everything: the stack fixtures, the cold plates, the pump that sounded wrong and was supposed to, the one that sounded right and wasn't. She'd written most of the test procedure. She'd run the qualification unit herself. She was the only person in the company who had ever run a full stack at Mars pressure.
At lunch, at a picnic table under the cottonwoods, he asked who her backup was.

For what? she said. Then she understood. There's a technician who's watched me twice. My manager thinks the procedure covers it. She looked at the chamber building. It doesn't. I haven't taken a week off since 2059.
Paloma is the only one who really knows the test. What's Sam's best move?
A. Have Peg require Rio Puerco to name two more qualified test engineers within thirty days.
B. Ask Paloma to skip vacation and travel until the test is done, for a completion bonus.
C. Fund a Tallgrass engineer to work beside Paloma on every chamber run from now on.
D. Offer Paloma a job at Tallgrass and bring the test knowledge in house with her.

By Monday a Tallgrass electrochemist named Desmond Ruiz, twenty nine, has a badge at Rio Puerco and a desk next to Paloma's. Rio Puerco's technician joins them. Paloma is suspicious for a day and then, it turns out, relieved, because she's been the only person to call at three in the morning for two years. They start a binder called WHAT PUMP 2 WANTS. Sam adds the arrangement to the resource plan and the risk register, and Peg Sato in contracts writes it into the statement of work so it survives a reorganization. On the flight home Sam reads the first page of the binder. It says, in Paloma's handwriting, If it sounds fine, check it anyway.

Exactly right. Manage resource availability before it fails. A single point of failure is a risk to the project and a burden on the person. Pair a backup with them on real work, capture the knowledge, and put the arrangement in the resource plan and the contract so it lasts.

Saturday, April 2. Garrett called the meeting for nine on a Saturday, which was a thing he did when he wanted people to know he meant it. He had Hale on the speaker in the middle of the table. She was in her car somewhere, and every so often a turn signal ticked under her voice.
I have the partners in May, Hale said. I'd like to tell them the program found a week. One week. I'm not asking for a miracle.

Garrett had a plan ready. The valve campaign at the stand ran in sequence before stage integration: test the valve, then build the stage around it. Overlap them. Start integrating the stage while the campaign runs. We get the stage ready three weeks early. Easy week.

Wendell was at the end of the table in his jacket. He hadn't been asked to come, and he'd come. If the campaign finds something, he said, the stage is already bolted together around it. Nobody said anything. He looked at Sam. Write down that I said that.
Sam wrote it in his notebook. Wendell watched him do it. Twice. Sam wrote it again, under the first one, and Wendell nodded once and looked out the window at the wind sock.

Quinn slid the crash table across to Sam without a word. On the Breather's critical path, lander integration could lose a week for $350,000. Plant assembly could lose one for $500,000. The software release could lose one for $200,000, but it had three weeks of float.
Hale wants a week back, Garrett has a plan, and Quinn has a crash table. What should Sam do?
A. Crash the software release for $200,000, the cheapest week on Quinn's crash table.
B. Crash lander integration for $350,000 and leave the valve campaign in sequence.
C. Tell Hale no safe week is available yet and hold the baselined schedule as it is.
D. Overlap the valve campaign with stage integration as Garrett proposes, for three weeks.

Sam tells Hale she can have one week, and what it costs, and where it comes from: a second integration crew on the lander for two weeks in August, $350,000 out of contingency, through the change board on Monday. The valve campaign stays in sequence. Garrett argues for ten minutes that the overlap is free. Sam turns the butcher paper around so he can see that the stand isn't on the critical path. So my three weeks were worth nothing. On the end date, nothing. On the risk, a lot. Hale says, One week, honestly bought. I can say that. Wendell gets up and leaves without a word, and on his way past Sam's chair he puts a hand on the back of it for a second.

That's a go. To shorten the schedule, compress the critical path, starting with the activity whose cost slope is lowest. Crashing lander integration buys a real week at a known price. Fast tracking the valve test adds rework risk, and the stand isn't critical, so it buys nothing at all.

Monday, April 4. The integration standup was fifteen minutes on a good day. This one was in its twenty fifth. The item was the valve command interface, the software that told MOIV-1 to open and close, and whether it was done.
It's done, Rafa said. It passed every case in the simulation. Four hundred cases. We're moving it to done on the board.
It's done when it's moved a real valve, Hana said. Your simulation thinks the valve closes in two hundred milliseconds every time. I have a report on my desk that says it doesn't always.
Then put your valve in my simulation.
I'd like it to stay on the stand, where it can't hurt anybody.

Everybody else at the standup was looking at the floor. Quinn had both hands flat on the table. It was the third Monday in a row they'd had some version of this, and the second time in a week the word done had meant two things in one room.
Hana and Rafa mean two different things by done. How should Sam settle it?
A. Split the rule: valve interfaces need a stand run, and the rest are done on simulation.
B. Keep both of them after standup and work out what done has to prove for each side.
C. Note both points, move the item to the parking lot, and get the standup back on time.
D. Rule for Hana that nothing touching a crit 1 valve is done until it runs on hardware.

Sam stops the standup and keeps the two of them afterward with Quinn and a whiteboard. He asks each of them what done has to prove, and writes their answers down side by side, and they turn out not to be opposites. Rafa needs the logic tested fast and often. Hana needs proof against the real valve's behavior, including the bad cycle. What they write: an interface is done when it passes the simulation, and the simulation includes the valve's measured response from the stand, and it's run once against the stand article before it's flagged flight ready. Rafa says the stand runs will slow him down. Hana offers him a weekly slot on the stand article, Tuesdays, which nobody has ever been offered. Quinn tapes the definition to the wall over the standup board. That's a ground rule, Rafa says. That's a ground rule, Hana says, at the same time, and they both look annoyed about it.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Find the source of the conflict, look at what each side actually needs, and work the problem until both needs are met. That's collaborating, and it fits real stakes with a little time. Then write the result down as a ground rule the team keeps, so the fight doesn't come back every Monday.
Tuesday, April 5. 6:10 AM. Paloma called Sam's cell from the chamber floor. He could hear the cottonwoods outside. He could also hear, behind her, the absence of a sound.

Pump 2 seized at three this morning. Bearing. We were in a checkout pump down, no stacks in, nobody hurt. The spare is six weeks out from the manufacturer. A pause. It's in your risk register. I watched Quinn write it down last week.
It was. Line 418. Chamber roughing pump failure, probability 2, owner Rio Puerco, response: monitor.

At 6:40, in the program room, Sam put it on the wall. The acceptance test was supposed to start May 16. Six weeks for a pump put the test into late June, and every day of it came straight off the critical path.

Wendell read the line over his shoulder. What model? Sam told him. Wendell was quiet for a second. There's one of those in ground support stores. Building 4, back corner. From the habitat thermal vac in '58. Nobody's turned it on in three years.
Pump 2 needs six weeks, and every day of it comes off the critical path. What should Sam do first?
A. Have Peg push the pump maker to expedite a new one under the Rio Puerco contract.
B. Ask Hale this morning to approve a second chamber at another supplier as a backup.
C. Open it as an issue and work out a fix this morning with everyone who might help.
D. Mark the risk as realized and review the response at Thursday's risk meeting.

By 7:30 Sam and Wendell are in Building 4 with a flashlight and a pallet jack. The pump is there, under a tarp, with a tag from 2058. Wendell plugs it into a test panel and listens to it for ten minutes with his eyes shut. She'll go. Paloma checks the flanges against the chamber drawings over video and says they match within a millimeter. By noon Peg has a loan agreement written and Rio Puerco's manager has signed it. The pump leaves Watkins on a flatbed at four and gets to Albuquerque at two in the morning, and Paloma is there in the dark to meet it. The issues log gets a new line with an owner and a date on it, and the risk register gets a note: issue opened, and a second spare pump added as a response. The critical path loses three days instead of six weeks.

Exactly right. Recognize when a risk becomes an issue, evaluate the impact of the impediment, and choose an intervention with the people who can help. Here the impact sat straight on the critical path, so it got worked within the hour. Then update the issue log and the register, and keep reassessing.
Tuesday, April 5, 3:00 PM. The program's first monthly status since the baseline was due to Hale and the board by Friday. It was also Sam's first status report on anything bigger than a building.

Quinn put the numbers on the wall in four lines. Stack fabrication was five working days late, on the critical path. The pump had cost three more. The software release was two weeks late, and it had started with three weeks of float. The stand was on its dates.

The lander week bought on Saturday was already promised to Hale for the partners, so it covered none of this. Net, the Breather's path was eight working days late against the baseline, with no float anywhere to absorb it.
The plan's threshold, written into it in February, said that any slip of five working days or more on the critical path went to the sponsor in writing.
Garrett had seen the wall on his way past. He stuck his head in. We're still inside the window, right? Then it's green.
Garrett says it's green as long as they're inside the window. What goes in the status report?
A. Report each team's percent complete, 61 overall, on the readiness board's standard template.
B. Mark the report green overall, with the launch still inside the window, per Garrett.
C. Report the critical path slip and its recovery plan, and leave the software slip out.
D. Report each slip against the baseline and what it does to the float and the forecast.

The report is one page and a chart. Each slip, its cause, whether it's critical, what float is left behind it. The forecast for the Breather's path, and what it does to the launch odds Hale already has. The plan: the pump recovery, a second spare pump on order, the stack line's shift plan. Under the software line Quinn writes Two weeks of float spent, one left. Watch. Sam sends it a day early. Hale's chief of staff replies at 9 PM. The Director says this status told her what to worry about. She says they usually don't. Garrett reads it in the morning and comes down to the program room. You put yellow on a page with my name on it. It was yellow. Garrett thinks about that for a moment and goes back upstairs.

That's a go. Assess current progress, measure it against the baseline, and communicate status in a form decision makers can use: each variance, its effect on the critical path and end date, the float left, the forecast, and what you're doing about it. Spent float belongs in the report.

Wednesday, April 6. 5:40 AM. One way light time was five minutes and fifteen seconds. Tomorrow morning it would bottom out and start climbing again, and Quinn's note on the program calendar would come down.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3601. One way, 5 minutes 15 seconds. Margin, 874 days. Hi, Dad. Sol 3601. Sorry about the hair. I've been up since 0300, so this is the hair you get. Everybody's fine. Start there. At 0300 the CO2 scrubber in Hab 2 tripped, and its backup didn't pick up, because of course it didn't. Eleven people asleep in there. The alarm went, and I was closest, so it was me and Teodor from the machine shop in our socks pulling the backup's controller board with the hab doors sealed. We got it running in nineteen minutes. That's well inside the limit. I want you to know it was well inside the limit. Nobody even had a headache. It's not an oxygen thing, so it doesn't change my number. It's just a sleep thing. (That's my hands. They're fine. They'll stop.). Your log about the valve. I watched it twice. I still don't know what you're not saying, and I can tell there's something. Okay. I need to tell you something, and you can't tell Hollis. Promise to the screen. I'll wait. Bay D. The old storage module past the greenhouse. Hollis said no to expanding into it in January because there aren't hours on the roster for it. So I've been doing it on my own hours. Teodor helps some nights, and a botanist named Pilar who doesn't sleep anyway. We've got racks in. We've got lights in. We've got the first trays of lettuce under them, and lettuce makes oxygen, Dad, not a lot, but it makes it. It's the only thing on this station that makes more air than it did last month. It isn't in my number. It won't be until it's finished, and I won't guess at it before then. I know what you're going to say about the hours. You'd say it to anybody else. Don't say it to me. You did nineteen years of nights in a building that wasn't even on fire. 874. Same minus nine as last time, I'm guessing. Love you. Go to work. Ada out.
He watched it twice. The second time he paused it on her hands, the way he had in January, and looked at them for a long while, and then let it play.

At 6:30 he was in the high bay. The stack line had been on two shifts since the critical path went up on the wall, and nobody had asked them to; they'd seen the paper and decided. At 4:10 that morning the twenty three year old technician had cross threaded a manifold fitting on stack six, a small brass part, easily fixed, and sat in her car in the lot afterward with the engine running and wouldn't come back in. Quinn had found her there at five and was sitting in the passenger seat now. The rest of the line sat at the bench in the lab at the far end of the high bay, the one that smelled like a swimming pool. Nobody was talking. Two of them hadn't been home since Sunday.
He thought about a car in a lot in Bennett in January with the engine running, and about Ada's hands.
The stack line is on double shifts, and a technician is out in her car. What should Sam do first?
A. Tell the line that the margin numbers are uncertain enough to give the colony more time.
B. Thank the line at shift change, buy breakfast, and remind them what the hours are for.
C. Have HR set a twelve hour shift limit for the stack line, starting with today's shift.
D. Pull up a stool at the bench and ask the stack line what the last week has been like.

He pulls up a stool at the bench and asks what the last week has been like, and then he doesn't talk for a while. It comes out slowly. They read the critical path. They read the margin on the news. They decided the colony dies if they're a day late, and nobody told them otherwise. When they're done he tells them what he knows: the path has a recovery plan, the days lost to a pump are only days, and a cross threaded fitting at four in the morning is how you lose a month. They agree on a pace together. No shift over ten hours, nobody past six days, and the line lead calls a stop any time. Sam tells them he'll carry the date to Hale and Garrett himself, and does that afternoon, with the new shift plan and its cost in days. The twenty three year old comes in at nine with Quinn. Nobody says anything about the car. The lead gives her stack six back, and she fixes the fitting herself, slowly, and gets it right.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Servant leadership: find out what the team is carrying, remove what's in their way, and set expectations with them, including a pace that's safe. Then represent their voice upward and take the date pressure yourself. A frightened team makes mistakes, and on a ship mistakes have mass.

Thursday, April 7. Commander Yusra Haddad came out from the training center in Aurora with a printout of the network folded to the bottom of the page, where crew training ran on its own long path. Six weeks of float. She'd circled the number in pen.

Rafa wants my simulator, she said. Three weeks in May, for the Breather code runs. Garrett's office called yesterday and said my float is going to be listed as program reserve in the investor deck. Nobody's asked me about either one. I found out from the deck.
Rafa was in the doorway behind her. The Breather's critical. The crew has six weeks. The sim is the only place we can run the control code against a full plant model.
And my crew has four people learning to install an oxygen plant on Mars from a manual nobody's written yet.
Quinn looked at Sam. Neither of them could remember the team ever agreeing whose float was whose, because they never had.
Rafa and Commander Haddad both want the crew path's float. How should Sam handle it?
A. Work out a rule with Haddad and Rafa for who decides when any float gets spent.
B. Hold the crew's six weeks himself as a schedule reserve he doesn't publish.
C. Give Rafa the simulator weeks in May out of the crew path's six weeks of float.
D. Let Commander Haddad decide, as the owner of the crew path and its simulator.

They write it in ten minutes on the whiteboard and Quinn types it up. Float belongs to the project. Anyone who wants to use it says so at standup, Quinn logs it, and the owners of both paths decide together, with Sam if they can't. Then Haddad and Rafa settle it, mostly without him. Rafa gets two weeks of simulator nights in May. The crew keeps the days. Haddad gets two of Rafa's engineers to help write the install procedures the crew needs. Sam calls Garrett's office himself and asks for the crew's float to come out of the investor deck. That's the first time anybody asked me about my own schedule, Haddad says on her way out. Mine too, Rafa says, and she gives him a look, and then she laughs.

Exactly right. Lead the team by setting expectations at the team level and empowering it: agree the ground rule, make float visible, and let the people who own the paths settle its use. Represent the team upward, including against a deck that quietly took its float.

Thursday, April 7. 8:10 PM. The envelope was in the mailbox, long and white, addressed in green ink, with a Golden postmark and no return address. Page three. Sam brought it in with the gas bill and a seed catalog and set it on the kitchen table against the fruit bowl, where it leaned and watched him make a sandwich.
He answered Ada first. He sat in his chair, not Grace's, under the bulb over the table, and pressed record. The bulb was still dying.

I promise to the screen. I won't tell Hollis. He held up his hand to the camera, and felt foolish, and kept it up. I'm also not going to say the thing about the hours. You're right. I'd say it to anybody else. He put the hand down. I'm going to ask you for three numbers instead. How long until Bay D is finished. If everything goes right, what you'd bet on, and if the bad things happen. I won't show anybody. I just want to know where my critical path is. He thought about it. It's you, by the way. It's been you the whole time. He didn't do the voice. He watched it back once, changed nothing, and sent it, and five minutes and fifteen seconds later it was on Mars, waiting for her morning.

Quinn's schedule on the big room wall said February 18, inside the window, with no float in front of it. It was the least encouraging thing Sam had ever signed, and he believed every line of it, and so, he'd noticed, did the people whose names were on the lines.
At 9:05 Quinn called. She didn't say hello. Have you seen the long range outlook?

He hadn't. She'd moved the second valve campaign up to its early start, the week of April 18, so that Wendell could sit Albuquerque in May. It had been the right call on paper and in the network, and it had given them their float back.

There's a storm coming off the Palmer Divide that week. Late season. They're saying it could be a big one. Wind, and a lot of snow, sideways. She was quiet. That's the only cold, dry week the stand gets before June. Hana checked the history. It's April or nothing.
He drove out. He didn't decide to; he was on I-70 with the heater on before he'd thought about it, and the envelope was on the passenger seat, face down, because he'd picked it up with his keys.

Wendell's truck was in the lot. It was always in the lot. Inside the blockhouse the four screens showed the stage under its blankets, and the wind was doing what it did out here, leaning on the walls hard enough that the coffee in the thermos lid on Wendell's knee shivered in rings.
April, Wendell said, before Sam had his jacket off.
Quinn says it's April or nothing.
Quinn's right. She's usually right. It's a bad habit in a scheduler.
They watched the screens. After a while Sam asked him why he'd wanted it written down twice, on Saturday.

Wendell turned the thermos lid around on his knee a full turn before he answered. So there's two, he said. One gets lost. He didn't say anything else, and Sam, who had spent nine years on flight lines with men who answered exactly the question you asked them, didn't ask a second one.

It had been a good ten days, by the numbers. He'd told the truth on a status report and bought a week honestly and found a pump under a tarp. He didn't trust the feeling any more than he had in March. It had a way of showing up right before weather.

At midnight he drove home. The envelope rode on the passenger seat, face down, the way the printout of AR 2207 had ridden out here in February. That morning, at 7:48, Mars had been as close as it would come before the ship left, five minutes and fifteen seconds away, and Quinn's note on the calendar had come down. He'd open page three at the kitchen table, where he opened all of them.
Not tonight. The wind came across the prairie with nothing to stop it between Watkins and Kansas, and somewhere south of the Palmer Divide, eleven days out, the weather was already deciding.
